representations.text:
Your March 30–April 12 records show a sustained shift from your 28-day baseline: sleep averaged 5h 31m versus 7h 49m, down 2h 18m (29%). Sleep started around 01:09 instead of 22:51, while waking stayed at 07:00. Steps fell from 7,985 to 2,643 daily (67%). Both changes persisted across all 14 days, including weekends, with no return toward baseline.

Other measures stayed close to your usual pattern: active time averaged 55 versus 54 minutes, still starting at 21:00; low movement averaged 451 versus 449 minutes. Resting heart rate edged from 55 early to 57 bpm late but remained within your baseline range; RMSSD averaged an unchanged 44.9 ms. Active time had only a weak relationship with the following night's sleep. All measurements were available. Tracking whether sleep timing and steps return toward your usual levels would clarify persistence.

Your clearest change during March 30–April 12 was how movement was distributed. Every day, including weekends, low-movement periods shortened from roughly 44–47 minutes to 15 minutes, with recorded one-minute movement bouts every 20 minutes from 10:16 to 20:16. Your 21:00 activity bout shortened to 19–28 minutes from 50–60 minutes. Total active time remained about 55 minutes daily, while total low movement increased from 449 to 480 minutes (+7%). More frequent interruptions therefore coexisted with more low movement overall; posture and intensity are unknown.

Steps averaged an essentially unchanged 8,038 versus 8,026, although they trended downward about 29 daily across the window, staying within baseline range. Sleep remained near 7h 51m, starting around 22:49 and ending at 07:00. Resting heart rate and RMSSD stayed near 55.9 bpm and 45.6 ms. Active time showed only a weak relationship with following-night sleep. No measurements were missing.

Your steps fell consistently during March 30–April 12: 6,433 daily on 13 recorded days versus 9,552 during your 28-day baseline, down 3,119 (33%). Every observed day was below the baseline range, including weekends, with no rebound and only a slight further downward trend. April 7 daytime measures are missing because wear coverage was insufficient; that day is not zero.

This step change was much larger than the change in active time, which averaged 53.5 versus 55.1 minutes, still starting at 21:00. Low movement remained close to baseline at 451 versus 448 minutes. Sleep stayed near 7h 50m, starting around 22:50 and ending at 07:00, with little weekday/weekend difference. Resting heart rate remained near 56 bpm; RMSSD averaged 45.5 versus 45.2 ms with less variability. Steps and active minutes showed virtually no daily relationship; active time had a modest inverse association with following-night sleep, without establishing causation.

Your sleep changed abruptly halfway through March 30–April 12. The first seven wake dates stayed near your 28-day baseline of 8h 01m. On April 6–12, sleep dropped to 5h 57m–6h 08m, averaging about 6h 03m—roughly 1h 58m below baseline. Sleep starts shifted from around 22:39 to 00:32–00:43, while waking remained at 07:00. This persisted through the final weekend without a return. The overall average of 7h 02m masks that distinct second-week change.

Steps stayed near 7,979 versus 7,976 daily, active time near 54 versus 56 minutes with bouts starting at 21:00, and low movement near 450 minutes. Resting heart rate remained around 56 bpm. RMSSD averaged 44.2 versus 45.3 ms, but was already lower before sleep shortened and did not decline alongside it. Active time had only a weak association with following-night sleep. No measurements were missing; continued recording can show whether the later sleep timing persists.
